covalent.note: Covalent radius; PubChem's values are those of Cordero et al., Dalton Trans. 2008, 2832. Value for l.s.; also 150(7)[h.s.].

vdw.note: Van der Waals radius (Los Alamos National Laboratory).

allen.note: Configuration energy (Allen electronegativity) in eV, not converted to the Pauling-like scale; Mann 2000b.

polarizability.note: Recommended value of the 2018 table: from experiment where it is precise enough, otherwise from high-level calculation.

crust.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for Earth's crust, via PubChem ('2.5×10¹ milligrams per kilogram').

ocean.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for sea water, via PubChem ('2×10⁻⁵ milligrams per liter').

solar.note: Proto-solar (4.567 Ga ago) elemental mass fraction, column 'Elemental Mass Fractions' of ESM Table A13; the table gives no uncertainty (relative sigma of N(E) in Table 6 applies). SOURCE INCONSISTENCY: Table A13 lists N(Si=1e6) = 2290 for Co but its mass fraction 4.073E-06 corresponds to N = 2260 (the isotopic-abundance column of the same row); Table 6 gives N = 2292 +- 116, i.e. ~1.3 % higher. Printed value kept; difference is well inside the 5 % sigma.

solarLogEps.note: A(E) = log10(N_E/N_H) + 12, 'Solar System Present' log (E/H)+12; basis: meteoritic (CI-chondrite) value; unc = 1 sigma in dex as printed.

body.note: In a 70 kg reference adult (ICRP Publication 23, 1975, Table 110).

temperature.note: The COD entry does not state the temperature of the measurement.

crystal.reference: Taylor, A.; Floyd, R. W. (1950). Acta Crystallographica 3, 285.
crystal.note: The CIF states only 'T < 450 C' (the hcp stability range); the actual measurement temperature is not given. Above that range cobalt is fcc.

tonnesPerYear.note: World mine production, cobalt content, 2025 (USGS: 310,000 metric tons).

unitValue.note: Price, average, dollars per pound: U.S. spot, cathode [Cobalt], 2025; per kg of the material named, as USGS gives it.

origin.note: Read off Fig. 39 at the dotted 'age of the Sun' line (t = 9.2 Gyr after the Big Bang, 4.6 Gyr ago): pixel fractions of the stacked areas (agb 0.148, massive_stars 0.570, white_dwarfs 0.283); quantised to 0.05. Stack height 42 px. Paper: 'For the elements from Ne to Ge, the newly synthesized amounts are very small for AGB stars, and the small green areas are mostly for mass loss.'

plantRole.text: Needed by the nitrogen-fixing bacteria in legume root nodules, which use it in vitamin B12 (cobalamin); not needed by the plant itself.

humanRole.text: The metal at the heart of vitamin B12, which we must take in already made.

biology.note: Human: EFSA sets its value for cobalamin (vitamin B12), not for cobalt itself.

iarc.agent: Cobalt metal (without tungsten carbide or other metal alloys)

history.nameOrigin: From the German Kobold, a goblin of mining folklore blamed for ores that gave no useful metal and gave off poisonous fumes.
history.note: Brandt showed that the blue colour of cobalt glass comes from this metal rather than from bismuth. Jefferson Lab gives 1739.

prose.text: Cobalt is a hard, bluish-silver metal and one of the few elements that are magnetic at room temperature; it gives glass and porcelain their deep 'cobalt blue' and sits in the cathodes of many lithium-ion batteries. Its name comes from the Kobold, a goblin that German miners blamed for ores that gave off poisonous arsenic fumes instead of useful metal. Cobalt is the metal at the heart of vitamin B₁₂, and the bacteria in legume root nodules need it to fix nitrogen. The atom, [Ar] 3d⁷ 4s² (ground term ⁴F₉/₂), has three unpaired d electrons, and its single stable isotope, cobalt-59, has nuclear spin 7/2.
